segments.say: Let's start with the part of the story that worked perfectly, which was recognising the face.

show.title: A face that arrives all at once

segments.say: When the man in the linen shirt stepped across the street, Marta knew him before he said a word. There was no searching, no effort, no moment of, hmm, where do I know that face from. The recognition simply arrived, whole, in a fraction of a second, and it brought a warm feeling along with it. That feeling is part of the answer, and we'll come back to it.

Think about how much face-reading you do in a single ordinary day. You glance at a stranger on a train and know in an instant whether they look familiar. You spot a friend in a crowded street from far away. You notice that someone looks tired, or pleased, or worried, without being told. All of this happens so smoothly that we hardly count it as a skill at all. It's just what eyes do.

Now compare that with names. Names don't arrive in a fraction of a second. They show up late, or they show up wrong, or they don't show up at all. They have a way of vanishing in exactly the moments when we want them most, usually in front of the person who owns them. Most of us have felt this so often that we've simply accepted it, like bad weather.

There's a line in the later research that captures the same idea. Looking back at a well-known diary study from the 1980s, one research team wrote that it appears names are peculiarly hard to recall. Not a little harder. Peculiarly hard. And the evidence behind that sentence is a lovely piece of everyday science, so let's look at how it was gathered.

show.text: It appears that names are peculiarly hard to recall.
show.by: How later researchers described the diary findings

segments.say: Here's the study. In 1985, three psychologists, Andrew Young, Dennis Hay and Andrew Ellis, asked 22 volunteers to keep diaries. For seven weeks, whenever they had any trouble recognising a person, they wrote it down. At the end, the researchers had collected more than 900 naturally occurring slips. It was a way of catching ordinary memory in the act, not in a laboratory but in real life.

show.where: A diary study of everyday slips
show.what: 22 people kept diaries for seven weeks, writing down every time they had trouble recognising someone. They collected over 900 incidents.

segments.say: Hold on to that number for a moment. More than nine hundred slips, from only twenty-two people, in just seven weeks. That tells you something important before we even look at what the slips were. Trouble with faces and names isn't rare, and it isn't a sign that something is wrong. It's happening, quietly, all around us, every week of our lives.

show.title: Young, Hay & Ellis, 1985
show.label: everyday recognition slips logged by 22 people in seven weeks

segments.say: The slips weren't all the same kind. The biggest group was mistaken identity. Of the 900 or so incidents, more than 300 were people taking one person for another. In 272 of them, someone unfamiliar had been mistaken for someone the diary keeper knew. So recognition isn't a perfect machine that only fumbles names. It's a quick, helpful guesser, and now and then it guesses a little too eagerly.

Marta's slip belongs to a different, very familiar family. She recognised the face. She knew who the man was, in every way that mattered to her. What she couldn't do was produce the word that goes with him. It's a kind of failure that feels enormous in the moment, and yet it leaves everything else about the person perfectly intact.

So, a short summary of what those diaries showed. Faces feel familiar quickly. Strangers are sometimes mistaken for friends. Names are the hardest part to produce. And people often know a good deal about someone, while the name stays out of reach. It's a very human pattern, and it's remarkably consistent from person to person.

show.title: What the diaries showed
items: Strangers are sometimes mistaken for friends
People often know everything but the name

segments.say: Here's what makes it a puzzle. A name is a tiny thing. A word or two, a handful of sounds. A face is enormously complicated, with thousands of tiny differences in shape, shade and expression. If you had to guess which of the two a brain would struggle with, you'd probably say the face. And yet, in everyday life, it's almost always the other way round.

Marta lies in the dark and thinks about this. She can picture the man's laugh lines and the slightly crooked collar of that linen shirt. She can picture the exact yellow of the bicycle. But a name of four or five letters is nowhere to be found. It seems almost unfair. Her mind has kept a hundred details and lost the simplest one.

Picture the street where it all began, now that the party is over. String lights still glow along the fence. A long table stands empty, with a few paper lanterns left on it. A few hours earlier this garden was full of faces, dozens of them, passing by in the lamplight. Marta recognised nearly every one of them without a moment's thought. The only word she lost was a single name.

show.cap: The street party, after everyone has gone

segments.say: Remember the warm feeling that came with the recognition? That's worth a moment. When Marta saw her neighbour, she didn't only recognise a face. She felt familiarity, a soft, glowing sense of, I know you. It's a feeling that arrives before facts and before names, and psychologists treat it as a distinct step on the way to knowing someone. We'll meet that step properly in a little while.

Here's a small thought experiment, if you'd like one. Think of a friend you see often. Notice how quickly their face appears in your mind, along with the sound of their voice and the feeling of being around them. Now think of their phone number, or the name of the street they grew up on. Notice how much more slowly and effortfully that comes, if it comes at all.

One way to picture the difference is this. Faces arrive like weather. You look up, and it's simply there. Names have to be fetched, like something from a high shelf in another room. And fetching takes a different kind of effort, which can fail even when the thing you're after is sitting right where you left it.

show.text: Faces arrive like weather. Names have to be fetched.

segments.say: It's worth saying a little more about why the diary method is so clever. Most memory research happens in laboratories, with lists of words and pictures on a screen. But everyday slips, the kind that happen at parties and on street corners, are hard to bring into a laboratory. So the researchers asked people to carry the laboratory with them, in the form of a small notebook, and to write down each slip the moment it happened.

A notebook like that captures things a laboratory never could. The slip with a neighbour in a corridor. The moment you waved at a stranger. The time you knew a colleague's job and her children's names, and not her own. It's rough data, and the researchers knew it had limits. But over seven weeks, from twenty-two people, it built up a surprisingly rich portrait of how recognition goes wrong in ordinary life.

If Marta had kept a diary like that, tonight's entry would be a classic. Person: neighbour. Face: recognised at once. Details: yellow bicycle, gate, violin. Name: not available. It would sit in the notebook alongside hundreds of others like it, from hundreds of other people at other parties. And that's the comforting part. Her slip isn't a one-off. It's a very common species of slip.

You could say that a notebook of such slips would read like a collection of small human comedies. Everyone in it is trying to do something perfectly reasonable, to greet a person, to remember a name, and everyone in it falls a little short, in the same few ways. There's something very warm about that. We're all making the same small mistakes, in the same small ways, and surviving them very well.

It would be easy to take all this as proof that something is wrong with our memories. But the research points in the opposite direction. This pattern turns up in nearly everyone, and it has reasons rooted in how the brain handles faces on one side, and words on the other. Understanding those reasons is the most comforting part of tonight, and we're about to start.
And to understand why Marta's recognition was so smooth, let's look at what faces are to a brain.
